question: The Regulation on New Genomic Techniques (NGTs) currently being negotiated is a dangerous attempt to deregulate European legislation on genetically modified organisms, paving the way for the circulation of ‘new genetically modified’ plants and food, without mandatory risk assessment, without full traceability and – in many cases – without labelling.

Despite communication efforts to draw a distinction, many scientific bodies point out that NGTs are a form of genetic modification and pose corresponding risks to health, the environment and biodiversity. The artificial distinction which places NGTs in ‘low risk categories’ lacks a scientific basis and ignores the long-term and cumulative effects on ecosystems.

Meanwhile, the uncontrolled spread of NGTs poses a direct threat to organic farming and GMO-free production. Small and medium-scale farmers in particular, in Greece for example, risk facing crop contamination, loss of certifications and increased reliance on patented seeds from a few multinationals. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.
How does it justify the undermining of the precautionary principle and of consumers’ right to information?
What concrete actions will it take to protect biodiversity, organic farming and rural independence?
How does it ensure that legislation does not serve the interests of agro-industrial lobbies to the detriment of public health and rural societies?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.3.

2026) The scientific evidence1 on which the Commission proposal2 was based, notably from the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), confirms that plants obtained by certain new genomic techniques (NGTs) do not pose new hazards compared to conventionally bred plants and that some of the modifications obtained through them can also occur naturally or through conventional breeding.

This justifies a proportionate approach based on the different risk profiles of NGT plants and is fully in line with the precautionary principle. A requirement to label as genetically modified organisms (GMOs) plants obtained by certain NGTs that are equivalent to conventionally bred ones would not be justified. No such requirement exists for GMO plants obtained by random mutagenesis.
Seed labelling will enable supply chains to exclude plants obtained with NGTs, with information also available in public registers and variety catalogues.

The provisional agreement reached by the co-legislators on 3 December 2025 requires the Commission to establish a programme for monitoring of intended and unintended impacts of NGT plants on human and animal health and the environment, including on biodiversity, and impact on environmental, economic and social sustainability and on organic agriculture.

The provisional agreement ensures a high level of safety for human and animal health and the environment by keeping NGT plants that could not have been obtained conventionally subject to GMO legislation.

To ensure that NGTs benefit all key users and stakeholders, the Commission will assess the impact of patents on plant breeding, breeders’ access to genetic resources, and farmers’ ability to obtain diverse seeds and will oversee a code of conduct on patent licensing and transparency.
1 The impact assessment accompanying the Commission legislative proposal for a regulation on plants obtained

by certain NGTs contains the relevant references to the scientific evidence underpinning the proposal: https://food.ec.europa.eu/document/download/f1142e86-43df-4791-9df2563e696c59cf_en?filename=gmo_biotech_ngt_ia_report.pdf. EFSA’s scientific opinions relating to NGTs are available here: https://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/topics/newgenomic-techniques. 2 COM(2023) 411 final.
